chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu Al-Hasan Al-Rida (peace be upon him), said:

I asked him about the one in Ihram who hunts prey out of ignorance. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is an expiation.' I said, 'What if it was an error?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And what is the error in your view?' I said, 'He throws at this palm tree and hits another palm tree.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, this is the error, and upon him is the expiation.'

I said, 'What if he deliberately caught a bird, slaughtered it while he was in Ihram?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is the expiation.' I said, 'Did you not say that error, ignorance, and deliberation are not equal? So for what reason does the deliberate one surpass the ignorant and the erring one?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He sinned and played with his religion.'

key_terms.إِحْرَام: State of consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in ruling between hunting in error versus hunting deliberately while in Ihram?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), the distinction between legal liability (kaffarah) and spiritual fault (ithm) is clarified: while ignorance, error, and deliberation all incur the same expiation for hunting, the deliberate act is uniquely condemned as 'playing with one's religion.' This highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that the severity of the sin lies not in the material penalty but in the conscious disregard for the sanctity of the state of Ihram.
